metadata.title: Total Cost, Overheads, and Unsold Stock
metadata.description: Include transport, repair, installation, and unusable inventory when finding the true transaction cost and target selling price.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the commercial relationship step by step, explain why each rate uses its base, show intermediate amounts, check signs and units, then practice transfer with misconception-specific retries.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 12 “Profit and Loss,” printed pages 374–425. Approved scope: Distinguish purchase cost from total outlay and include stated overheads such as transport, repair, or installation in the cost basis. Handle production batches where all units cost money but some remain unsold or useless, calculating total revenue and profit against total outlay. Teach the denominator and unit checks and avoid counting costs twice. Base the lesson on solved example 10 and objective problems that explicitly add expenses or unsold units.

content.text: Total Cost, Overheads, and Unsold Stock: Include transport, repair, installation, and unusable inventory when finding the true transaction cost and target selling price. We establish the model, explain each step, and practice with targeted feedback.
The purchase invoice is not always the full cost of a transaction. Freight, repair, installation, packaging, and other stated expenses increase the amount invested in making the goods ready to sell.
Total cost=purchase cost+relevant overheads. If a television costs ₹12,500 and transport/installation total ₹1,100, the amount to recover before profit is ₹13,600.

A target margin is applied to this full outlay. For 15% profit on ₹13,600, the required total receipt is 1.15×13,600=₹15,640. Dividing by the number of items gives a per-item price only if all units sell at that price.

Separate expenses from revenue. A repair bill paid after purchase is part of cost; money received from customers is sales revenue. Profit is revenue minus total outlay, not revenue minus the invoice alone.
Batch production can create a trap: all units may incur cost even if some are unsold or unusable. If 800 units cost ₹1.50 each, total cost is ₹1,200 regardless of how many can be sold.
When only part of a batch sells, revenue is sold quantity times unit SP. Compare that revenue with the cost of the entire batch if the unsold stock has no value.

Suppose a maker sets a price so selling 600 units covers cost plus 30%, but actually sells 620. Find the implied unit price from the first condition, then multiply by 620 and compare with total outlay.
If leftover units have a salvage value, include that recovery in revenue. If the question says they are useless, their revenue is zero; do not silently assign them a resale value.
Do not add an expense twice. A stated “total cost including delivery” already contains delivery; an explicit separate repair cost should be added only once.
For several types of overhead, use a short cost table: purchase, transport, repair, installation, total. This keeps each currency amount visible and avoids dropping a small charge.
If overhead is a percentage of purchase cost, calculate that amount on the stated base before adding it. A 12% overhead on ₹150 is ₹18, making total cost ₹168.
A percentage profit on total cost differs from a percentage markup on purchase price when overhead exists. Always use the base named by the problem and state it in the final answer.
Check unit consistency: a per-item cost must be multiplied by units; a total transport bill is already a batch amount. The final CP and SP being compared must cover the same batch.
A revenue below total cost implies a loss even if each item was sold above its purchase invoice. This can happen when omitted overheads are large.
Before accepting a result, reconcile the ledger: opening investment + costs paid = total cost; total receipts + salvage = revenue; revenue−cost = net result.
